newsitem.title: FRANCE: French anti-racists fight extreme right, police.
newsitem.headline: French anti-racists fight extreme right, police.

text.p: Anti-racist militants clashed with members of France's extreme-right National Front (FN) party on Monday during a Bastille Day parade in the southern port of Toulon, eyewitnesses said.
Police in Toulon, whose mayor is from the anti-immigration Front, backed the rightists in the scuffles, the witnesses said. There were no immediate reports of serious injuries or arrests.
FN leader Jean-Marie Le Pen was reported to have been present on the reviewing stand when the incidents took place.

The fighting began when Fode Sylla, head of the SOS-Racisme anti-racist group, who was also invited to watch the parade by FN mayor Jean-Marie Le Chevallier, showed up with about 50 members of his movement.
The eyewitnesses said blows were exchanged as the anti-racists chanted "Liberty, Equality, Fraternity" in reply to shouts of "Le Pen president."
They said Sylla was physically assaulted by both rightists and policemen while FN sympathisers shouted that immigrants should be thrown into the sea.
Trouble had been expected after Sylla said his group would defy a ban by Le Chevallier to go ahead with a planned Bastille Day festival in the city later in the day.
The African-born Sylla said Le Chevallier had no grounds for banning the long-planned open-air event.
Le Chevallier, who initially cited a threat to public order, told Reuters he had given prior permission for a jazz festival on the same site.
But Sylla urged residents to defy the ban and up to 3,000 anti-racist militants later paraded through the town while passers-by shouted insults at them.
The anti-racists finally held their rally unopposed. Le Chevallier asked national police to break it up but authorities declined to act in order to avoid further disturbances.

Racism and immigration are emotive and contentious issues in French politics. Earlier, in a clear attack on the Socialist-led government, conservative President Jacques Chirac criticised moves to relax immigration laws, saying to do so would encourage more illegal immigrants.
"The employment and social situation does not allow our country to do this...and it would feed those xenophobic and racist reactions which I hate," Chirac said in a television interview.

The National Front, which advocates sending home three million immigrants and limiting jobs, social services and public housing to native-born French people, has long been at loggerheads with SOS-Racisme.
The movement has brought private prosecutions against Le Pen for espousing the theory of racial inequality and making ethnic slurs.
Le Pen was recently fined for calling Sylla a "mad, fat ox".
